value: 0.25 m/s2 pp at 500 Hz (lowest worker threshold)
eye: receptor not identified (whole-animal behavioural response; workers)
method: behavioural threshold to substrate-borne vibration pulses against sham stimuli
conditions: Caste: workers. Behavioural test: pulses of substrate-borne vibration in arenas on vibrational exciters, real versus sham stimuli in pseudorandom order; threshold is the lowest tested amplitude with significantly more reactions to real than sham stimuli; reaction is any change in behaviour from baseline (freezing at the highest amplitudes, antenna lowering at lower ones). Frequencies tested 350, 400, 450 and 500 Hz; amplitudes measured with LDV-calibrated accelerometers. Queens came from 28 nucleus colonies, workers and drones from 4 colonies; per frequency 15 virgin queens, 13 laying queens, 20 workers and 30 drones. Temperature not reported. Workers were always tested in pairs; virgin queens, laying queens and drones were tested alone in the petri dish, so caste comparisons cross caste with social context.

source.title: Sex and caste effects on the vibrational sensitivity in honey bees (Apis mellifera)

quote: The lowest thresholds found in virgin queens and in workers at 500 Hz were 0.25 m/s2 pp.
note: Caste-specific record: Apis mellifera (GBIF ACCEPTED, Apis mellifera Linnaeus, 1758). Acceleration unit printed as m/s2; the Results print 'pp' after it and the paper never defines pp, so peak-to-peak is not confirmed. Context from the same paper: workers and drones were tested in separate groups at each frequency; sensitivity was higher at 500 Hz for all groups; virgin queens had a constant threshold across frequencies; the freezing response threshold in workers was constant across the four frequencies at 0.5 m/s2 pp; drones were significantly the least sensitive and laying queens less sensitive than virgin queens. The receptor organ is not identified in this paper. Frequency range tested is 350 to 500 Hz only, the band virgin queens use, so lower-frequency sensitivity is not covered.

value: a sound stimulus 1000 ms before the air puff raised the jumping ratio to 39% of responding trials, significantly above control
eye: receptor not identified in this paper (tympanal ears not examined)
method: behavioural modulation of wind-evoked escape by a preceding 15-kHz tone at 70 dB SPL; not an audiogram
conditions: Behavioural test: adult male crickets (under 14 days after the imaginal molt, reared at 27 C, 12:12 h light/dark), tested in the dark phase at room temperature (26 to 28 C); each stimulus-pattern group had 15 individuals, 60 crickets in all. A 200 ms air puff (nitrogen from a 15 mm nozzle) was given alone or after a 200 ms 15-kHz pure tone at 70 dB SPL, with tone-to-puff delays of 0, 200, 1000 and 2000 ms. Control jumping share was 21% of responding trials; with the tone at 0, 200 and 2000 ms before the puff the jump ratios were 19%, 25% and 22%, almost the same as control, so only the 1000 ms delay changed jumping (Results 3.1).

source.authors: Lu A, Fukutomi M, Shidara H, Ogawa H
source.title: Persistence of auditory modulation of wind-induced escape behavior in crickets

where: Results, 3.1 Preceding high-frequency sounds increased the choice of jumping response
quote: When the sound stimulus was applied 1000 ms before the air puff in Pattern 3, the jumping ratio to all responding trials was 39%, which was significantly higher than that in the control.
note: Printed and accepted name Gryllus bimaculatus (GBIF ACCEPTED, De Geer, 1773, Gryllidae, Orthoptera). The study is about how a preceding tone changes the escape, so neither airflow nor hearing thresholds were measured. Context from the same paper: the preceding tone did not change the probability of responding to the puff, reaction time, maximum running velocity and distance were not different from control for any delay, tones at 0, 200 and 2000 ms delays left the jumping ratio at control level, the effect on running direction lasted at least about 800 ms after the tone and was gone at 1800 ms, and 5 kHz was not tested here. The receptor organs are not identified or manipulated in this paper. Only one tone frequency and level was used, so this gives no hearing range or best frequency.
